findings.title: Footfall is draining away while volume grows
findings.evidence: Scanned lines per trading day fell 17% across the three years, yet kilos sold ROSE 19%. Fewer, larger purchases. Revenue per day still ended -9% because price per kilo fell 23%. A counter can survive losing transactions while each remaining one grows -- right up until the point it cannot.
findings.action: Put lines per day on the same chart as revenue and watch it weekly -- no revenue-only report would have shown this. Read it as produce sales rather than shoppers, though: this data sees one counter. Store-wide till counts would say which it is, and that is the first thing to go and get.

findings.title: Spoilage is not priced in, anywhere
findings.evidence: RMB 239,699 of book profit over three years never existed -- it was stock bought and binned, 19.3% of everything the till reported as profit. The correlation between an item's loss rate and its markup is +0.047: pricing ignores spoilage completely. A vegetable that bins a quarter of its stock carries the same markup as one that bins none.
findings.action: Set price from loss-adjusted cost -- cost / (1 - loss rate) -- then apply the target margin. On a 25%-loss line that is about a third more markup than today. It is one formula in the pricing sheet and it is the highest-value change available in this dataset.

findings.title: Waste is concentrated in the best sellers, not the worst
findings.evidence: The top 10 items by waste cost carry 44.4% of all spoilage cost. Only 2 items actually flip from profit to loss -- the damage is volume multiplied by loss rate, so it lands hardest on the lines the shop sells most of. The two worst (Xixia Mushroom (1) and Broccoli) waste RMB 40,750 between them -- 3.0x the true profit earned by the entire bottom half of the range.
findings.action: Attack the short list, not the long one. For those ten lines specifically: smaller and more frequent deliveries, cold-chain and handling checks, and loss-adjusted pricing. A single point of loss rate recovered on Broccoli is worth more than delisting fifty dead SKUs.

findings.title: The range has a long dead tail nobody has reviewed
findings.evidence: 60 items sold on ten days or fewer in three years, and 110 have not sold at all in the final six months. The bottom half of the range contributes about 1% of revenue. These are not failing products so much as decisions made once and never revisited.
findings.action: Run a quarterly range review with a hard rule: no sale in 90 days is a delist unless someone signs to keep it. The gain is not the revenue -- there is none -- it is the ordering attention and shelf space returned to the top decile, which is volume-constrained rather than demand-constrained.

findings.title: Clearance works; the ordering that makes it necessary does not
findings.evidence: 5.4% of lines are marked down, overwhelmingly after 19:00 (27% of lines in the 21:00 hour). Those markdowns still return 9.7% true margin, so the discount mechanism is doing its job -- recovering cash from stock that would otherwise be binned entirely.
findings.action: Leave the markdown alone and fix what feeds it. Order to the hour profile rather than the day total: a heavy delivery before 09:00 for the morning market and a light top-up before 16:00 for the evening rush. The evening clearance pile is the visible end of a morning over-order.

findings.title: The last trading hour does not pay for itself -- at this counter
findings.evidence: After 21:00 the produce counter takes 2.1% of revenue at 24.9% margin, against about 30% through the rest of the day. It is simultaneously the thinnest and the least profitable hour, and the most heavily discounted.
findings.action: Move the staffed produce hour from 21:00 to the 09:00-11:00 peak, which carries a quarter of all revenue at full margin. A roster change, not a closing time -- this data only sees the produce counter, so if the rest of the shop trades late, the answer is a pre-packed section after 21:00.

findings.title: The single biggest sales event of the year is fully predictable
findings.evidence: 8 of the ten best days in three years fall in the week before Chinese New Year, and the best single day took 10x the median day. The peak is a calendar event, not a weekend effect.
findings.action: Plan it twelve months ahead -- ordering, staffing, cash handling and cold storage. There is no forecasting difficulty here: the date is known years in advance and the shape repeats in all three years of this data.
